title: Non-null assertion (!) and when it is dangerous
hook: The postfix exclamation mark tells TypeScript you guarantee a value is not null or undefined — but it emits nothing at runtime. Abuse of ! is a top rejection signal in senior interviews because it silences the compiler without adding safety.

blocks.text: The **non-null assertion operator** (`!`) removes `null` and `undefined` from a type for the checker: `value!` is typed as `T` when `value` was `T | null | undefined`. It compiles to **no JavaScript** — if your guarantee is wrong, you get a runtime `TypeError`. Common uses: DOM elements after mount, class fields initialized in constructor (with definite assignment), and legacy interop. Prefer **narrowing** (`if (x != null)`), **optional chaining** (`?.`), or **assertion functions** (`asserts x is T`) instead.

entries.plainDefinition: Postfix ! tells compiler value is non-nullish — no runtime check.
Different operator — casts type shape, can also use ! on postfix.
Function that throws if check fails — safer than !.
entries.example: function assertUser(x: unknown): asserts x is User

blocks.text: Codebases with `!` on every line defeated strictNullChecks for a false sense of safety. Production crashes from `null!` patterns rank high in postmortems. C# has `!` null-forgiving operator with the same compile-only semantics. ESLint `@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion` bans it in strict teams. Legitimate use: invariant you can prove (React root element exists) with immediate throw fallback.

blocks.title: ! is not a runtime guard
blocks.body: Emitted JS is identical with or without !. Only the compiler is fooled.

items.title: Prefer narrowing
items.body: if (el) { el.focus(); } — compiler and runtime agree.

items.title: Prefer ?? throw
items.body: const el = getEl() ?? throw new Error('missing');

items.title: Acceptable !
items.body: Framework invariant (Angular #app always exists) + test coverage.

items.title: Never !
items.body: API responses, user input, database nullable columns.

diagram.title: Non-null assertion vs narrowing
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  V[T | null | undefined] --> N{if x != null}
  N -->|yes| SAFE[Use x safely]
  V --> BANG[x!]
  BANG -->|wrong| CRASH[Runtime TypeError]
  BANG -->|right| SAFE

snippet.label: Dangerous — API data
snippet.explanation: Line 12: ! assumes user exists — 404 returns null and .name throws. Fix: if (user) guard.

snippet.label: Safe alternative — narrowing
snippet.explanation: Lines 3–5: explicit null check — compiler narrows user to User in else branch.

snippet.label: DOM — acceptable with fallback
snippet.explanation: Throw on missing element gives clear error. ! would crash with obscure null reference.

snippet.label: Assertion function — safer pattern
snippet.explanation: asserts value is T: compiler narrows after call; runtime throws on violation — better than silent !.

blocks.title: Chaining !
blocks.body: user!.profile!.email! — three lies. Use ?. or validate once at boundary.

blocks.text: Definite assignment assertion on class fields (`name!: string`) tells compiler constructor initializes — still no runtime check. Optional chaining with ! is redundant (`obj?.prop!`). In code review, ! count is a complexity metric. Migration from strict-off codebases: replace ! with narrowing in batches. C# null-forgiving after null check is the same trust-me pattern.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected
blocks.body: Defaulting to ! to silence errors. Thinking ! adds a runtime check. Using ! on fetch/JSON results.

interviewTakeaways: ! removes null/undefined from compile-time type only — zero runtime effect.
Prefer narrowing, ?., ?? throw, or assertion functions.
Legitimate !: proven invariants with tests — not API data.
60s: ! is compile-time trust me. No JS emitted. C# has same pattern. Ban in lint for APIs. Use if-guards or asserts for safety.
Follow-up: definite assignment assertion on class fields?
commonPitfalls: Weak: ! makes code null-safe at runtime — it does not.
Weak: sprinkling ! to pass tsc — hides real null risks.
Strong: Narrow or assert with throw. ! only for framework invariants. ESLint ban for teams.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS has no ! — you always need runtime if-checks. TS ! only appeases the checker.
asserts x is T gives compiler narrowing plus runtime validation — preferred over !.
